faq: What does this tool calculate?
The Unix timestamp (seconds since January 1, 1970, 00:00 UTC) for a local date and time in a stated zone.
Do I need an account?
No — time in, number out.
Can I use the result for professional work?
Yes — it is the standard conversion your systems perform; the zone is explicit, which is where professional errors usually hide.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — nothing here locates you; the zone is chosen, not detected.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Zone names are the IANA database's; other tools may label the same rules differently while computing the same instant.
Seconds or milliseconds?
This converter gives seconds. JavaScript timestamps are milliseconds — multiply by 1,000 when feeding those systems, and divide when reading theirs.
What about times before 1970?
Negative timestamps result, correctly. The arithmetic does not fear history.
Daylight saving gaps?

A local time inside the spring-forward gap (2:30 a.m. on changeover night) never occurred. Converters resolve it by rule; professionals avoid scheduling inside the gap — the converter's zone honesty exposes exactly such traps.
Leap seconds?
Unix time ignores them by construction (it pretends they don't exist). Astronomical precision is a different discipline.
Microseconds?
Some systems stamp microseconds (16 digits). Convert seconds here, then append the precision separately — mixing precisions inline is how off-by-a-million bugs are born.
Time zones by abbreviation?
Abbreviations collide (IST x3). The converter wants a real zone or place so the instant is unambiguous.
